transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I, um... well, I decided to make an appointment because I've just been dealing with this... this situation, I guess you could call it. It’s a bit hard to explain, really, but even on my better days—the days where I’m actually feeling okay and trying to just go about my normal routine—I just can't shake this awful feeling. 

You see, I’m very active in my community, or at least I try to be. I go to church every Sunday, have for decades, and I belong to a little walking club. We mostly just walk the mall on Tuesday and Thursday mornings to keep our joints moving, you know how it is. But lately... well, I’ve noticed that some of the people at church, and the ladies in the walking club, too, they’re... they're watching me. I catch them looking at me all the time. 

And, um, it’s not just the staring. They’ve started putting these little messages about me in the church bulletin. The paper one the ushers hand out at the doors? I'll be reading the weekly announcements and there will just be these phrases slipped in that I know are directed exactly at me. And the walking club ladies do it too, except they do it out loud. They’ll be chatting about something completely ordinary, like the weather or a sale, but the specific words they use... they’re actually hiding little messages about me in what they say. I just don't understand why they're all doing it, and it’s been weighing on me so much, I just... I just don't know what to do about it anymore.
Have you ever heard these messages or comments directly, without reading them or someone saying them out loud to you?

Well, yes, actually. I'm so glad you asked that, because I was just thinking about this the other day and wondering if I was just getting overly tired. You know how it is when you've been on your feet all day, maybe doing a bit too much housework, and your mind just sort of plays tricks on you? But no, it's not just when I'm tired. It happens mostly when I'm at home, and the house is perfectly quiet. My husband passed away five years ago—bless his heart, he was a good man, worked at the post office for thirty years—so it's just me in the house now. And sometimes, usually in the late afternoon when the sun is just starting to go down and it gets real still inside, I'll hear something. 

It's not like a booming voice from the sky or anything dramatic like you see on television. It's just... well, it sounds exactly like one of the ladies from the walking club, usually Martha or sometimes Susan. I'll be sitting in the living room, maybe doing a little knitting or just resting my eyes, and I'll hear my name, plain as day, coming from the kitchen. Or sometimes it sounds like it's coming from out on the back porch. It's just a few words, maybe "Margaret, are you there?" or "Margaret, did you see this?" 

And it's so clear, Doctor, it's so incredibly clear that I actually answer back! I'll call out, "Yes, Martha, I'm in the living room!" or I'll actually get up and walk all the way into the kitchen, expecting to see her standing by the sink. I even check the back door sometimes, thinking maybe she came by to drop off a recipe or something and didn't want to ring the bell. But then I get there, and of course, the room is completely empty. The door is locked. There's nobody there at all. And I just stand there feeling so foolish, realizing I've been talking to the air. It really startles me every time, because for that split second, I am absolutely certain someone is in my house speaking to me. It's very unsettling, especially when I'm already so worried about what they're saying about me at the mall and in the church bulletin.
Have you experienced any particularly stressful or traumatic events in your life, aside from the loss of your husband?

Well, aside from my husband... oh, goodness, yes. It’s funny you ask that, because it really does feel like it’s just been one thing after another sometimes. You get to a certain age, Doctor, and it seems like you’re suddenly going to more funerals than weddings, if you know what I mean. But, yes, there was something else that was very, very hard for me. My dearest friend... her name was Helen. 

Oh, Helen and I had known each other since our girls were in the Brownies together back in the seventies. We did absolutely everything together, especially after my husband passed. We’d bake, we’d go down to the garden center just to look at the hydrangeas, or we’d just sit on my back porch and talk for hours over iced tea. But then she got sick. It was very sudden—something with her heart, the doctors said, though her daughter never did give me all the exact details, which always bothered me a little bit, to be honest. But she passed away. That was about a year and five months ago. 

It was just devastating. Truly heartbreaking. I felt so completely lost without her, like a whole piece of my daily life was just carved right out, leaving this big empty space in my week. And you know, now that I’m really thinking about it and putting the timeline together in my head... all of this that I've been telling you about. The ladies at the walking club, the messages tucked into the church bulletin, hearing Martha's voice in the quiet of the kitchen... this has all been going on since not long after my close friend died. 

Yes, about a year and five months ago is when it all really started. I remember because it was right around the time I was finally trying to force myself to get back into my normal routine, going back to Sunday service and walking the mall without Helen there beside me. And that’s exactly when I first started noticing the looks, and the little comments they were hiding in their conversations. I just couldn't understand why they would be doing that to me when I was already grieving so much, you know? It just made everything so much harder, trying to mourn Helen while dealing with all these secret messages...

Are the messages you hear or read about yourself, whether in the church bulletin, from the walking club ladies, or the voices at home, focused on any particular aspect of your life or are they more general?

Well, Doctor, that is a very good question, and I've tried so hard to pin it down myself. The thing is, it’s terribly difficult for me to articulate it to anyone. When I actually try to explain things—like what the messages are saying or what they mean—it just... well, it gets so incredibly complicated. 

I’ll try to tell someone, maybe my neighbor Mrs. Gable when she comes over to borrow a cup of sugar, and I'll start with just one simple thought. I'll start by talking about the mail, maybe, or something specific from the church service, just trying to lay out plain and simple what I think the ladies are hinting at. But then... oh, it's so frustrating, Doctor... my words just sort of wander right off the path. I'll start with the church or the mail, and before I even realize what's happening, I end up talking about these old quilt patterns I used to sew. The log cabin ones, you know, or the double wedding ring pattern which is so terribly difficult to get the corners right on. 

And from the quilts, suddenly I'm going on about the birds out at my backyard feeder, the blue jays and how they make that awful screeching sound, and then somehow I'm talking about warnings. Just... warnings about things, like the birds are trying to tell me something, or the quilts mean something. And I'll be going on and on about the quilt patterns and the birds and the warnings, and I'll look over at Mrs. Gable, and she just has this completely blank look on her face. I can see it in her eyes that she doesn't have the faintest idea what I'm getting at. It's like I started driving on a paved highway and ended up deep in the woods, and I don't even know how I got there. 

So when you ask if the messages are general or specific, I suppose I just... I want to tell you exactly what they're focused on, I really do, but every time I try to explain it out loud, I just lose the thread completely and confuse everyone, including myself.
Are the messages you hear or read about yourself ever critical or threatening towards you?

Well, critical... yes, I suppose you could say that, but maybe not in the way of someone shouting at you or threatening to hurt you. It’s more like... well, it feels like they know exactly what’s already weighing so heavily on my heart. Because, Doctor, I just... I keep going over every little thing I might have done wrong in my life. It just loops around and around in my head, especially when the house is so quiet and I have too much time to think. 

I think about Helen constantly, and I just agonize over those last few months before she passed. I sit in my chair and I think about how I should have called her more. Why didn't I pick up the phone more often? There were days when my arthritis was acting up or I was just feeling a bit tired, and I didn't call, and now I just feel like I must have failed her. I really do. I failed my dearest friend when she probably needed me the most, and honestly, I feel like I must have failed everybody else in my life, too. My husband, my neighbors, everyone.

It’s just this awful, heavy feeling of being completely worthless, like I haven't done right by anyone. I’ll go over every single conversation Helen and I had, every time I didn't go over to her house when I could have, and it just eats away at me. So when I hear my name from the kitchen, or I see those little hints in the church bulletin, I can't help but feel like they are judging me for all of that. Like they all know what a terrible job I did as a friend. They know I let her down, and they're just reminding me of how much I failed. It’s so exhausting carrying all this guilt around, Doctor, it really is, and having the ladies at the walking club or the messages in the bulletin point it out just makes me feel even smaller.
Have you ever considered the possibility that the messages you're hearing or seeing might not be real or might not be about you?

Well, Doctor... I know why you're asking that. I really do. And believe me, I have sat at my kitchen table, with my hands wrapped around a warm mug of chamomile tea—which Helen always used to say was the absolute best thing for a worried mind—and I have tried to tell myself exactly that. I’ve looked right at the church bulletin, the one with the little blue cross on the front that Pastor Miller started using last spring, and I've said out loud to the empty room, 'Now you listen here, you are just imagining things. It's just a regular announcement about the choir practice or the spring bake sale.' I really, truly try to convince myself that I'm just a silly old woman making a mountain out of a molehill, just letting my imagination run away with me because I've been so terribly sad.

But... well, that's exactly why I finally came in to see you. Because no matter how hard I try to reason with myself, no matter how much I try to brush it off, even on my better days... and I do have them, you know, days where the house doesn't feel quite so heavy and I can actually manage to water my African violets and maybe open the blinds to let some sun in... even on those better days, I just absolutely cannot shake the feeling. 

I just can't shake it. I know that some of those people at church, and especially those ladies in the walking club, are watching me. I can feel their eyes on me when I'm just trying to get my steps in near the mall food court. And I know they are putting little messages about me in that bulletin, or slipping them into what they say to each other when they think I'm just a few paces behind them. It's just so clear to me, even when I try to pretend it isn't. I'll hear a certain word they use, or see the way a sentence is phrased in the Sunday announcements, and it just clicks. I know it's about me. So, I suppose I have tried to consider that it might not be real, but how can I ignore it when it feels so incredibly real? It's just right there in front of me, day after day, and it makes it so hard to just go about my normal life.
Can you tell me more about what you mean by the messages being complicated and how your thoughts seem to wander off when trying to explain them?

Well, Doctor, like I was mentioning earlier, it is just the most frustrating thing in the world, and I do apologize if I am repeating myself, but it is just so hard to live with. I really do sit down with every intention of being perfectly clear. I will think to myself, I am just going to explain exactly what they meant in the church bulletin this Sunday, or I am going to talk about the mail and how it was sorted. Just something simple, something plain. 

But as soon as I open my mouth, it is like my brain just takes the steering wheel and drives right off into the weeds. I start with the church or the mail, and then a word I say will remind me of something else, and suddenly I am talking about those quilt patterns again. And not just mentioning them in passing, but really going on and on about the stitching and the fabric, and then that reminds me of sitting by the window sewing, which makes me think of the birds at the feeder, and then the screeching, and then the warnings. 

It all feels so incredibly connected in my head right at that very second, like the quilts and the birds and the messages in the bulletin are all part of the same big knot. I feel like I am explaining it perfectly. But then I will take a breath and look over at whoever is listening to me, and I can just see it in their eyes. They are completely lost. They do not have the faintest clue what I am getting at. Poor Mrs. Gable just stands there looking at me like I am speaking a completely different language. It makes me feel so foolish, it really does. I just want them to understand the messages I am seeing, to know what I am carrying around all day, but instead, I just confuse them. And honestly, Doctor, by the time I am done talking and I see that blank look on their faces, I realize I have completely lost my own train of thought too.
When you're explaining these messages to someone, do you find that your thoughts jump from one idea to another that doesn't seem directly related?

Yes, Doctor, exactly like I was just saying a moment ago. That is exactly what happens, and it is just so incredibly frustrating. I will start out with every intention of just talking about one specific thing—like a thought about the mail and how the envelopes were stacked, or maybe that little note in the church bulletin. Something very simple and straightforward, or so I think. 

But then... well, it’s like my mouth just runs entirely away from me. I'll start on the mail or the church, and then suddenly, out of nowhere, I end up talking about those old quilt patterns I used to make. And not just a passing mention, but going on and on about the colors and the stitching, which then somehow makes me think of the birds out at the feeder, and the way they screech, and the warnings I feel like I'm getting from all of it. 

To me, in that exact moment, it feels like it all makes perfect sense together, like it's all one big story. But I know it doesn't seem directly related to anyone else. I can see it plain as day. I will be halfway through explaining the birds and the warnings, and I will look at the person I am talking to—like poor Mrs. Gable just the other Tuesday, right after the trash was collected—and I can see they just absolutely do not know what I am getting at. Their eyes just sort of glaze over, or they give me this polite little nod, but they are completely lost. It makes me feel so terribly flustered because I really do want to explain things clearly, I truly do, but my thoughts just jump and jump until neither of us knows how I got from the Sunday announcements to the bird feeder.
Do you find it difficult to stay focused on one topic when talking about the messages you're receiving?

Oh, goodness, yes. I know I am probably sounding like a broken record here, repeating myself so much about the exact same things, but that is really the honest truth of it. It is terribly difficult for me to just stay on a single track, no matter how hard I try to keep my thoughts neatly organized. 

It is just like trying to hold onto water with your bare hands. I will sit there, maybe holding a piece of mail—like the electric bill, or one of those glossy flyers for the grocery store—and I will think to myself, 'Now, just tell them about the flyer. Just stick to the flyer.' But my focus just slips right through my fingers. When I try to explain things, I really do start with just that one simple thought about the mail, or the church bulletin, but before I even realize what is happening, I have completely wandered off the path. 

It is like a loose thread on a sweater. I pull one little piece, and suddenly the whole thing unravels, and there I am, talking all about those quilt patterns I used to sew back when my husband was still alive, and then the birds at the feeder, and those terrible warnings I feel like I'm getting from the screeching. My mind just leaps from one stone to the next across the river, and I can't seem to stop and just stand still on one of them. And I just keep talking, thinking I am tying it all together beautifully, but then I look up and I can see it plain as day on their faces—they absolutely do not know what I am getting at. It makes me feel so scattered and embarrassed, because I really do want to just stay on the one topic, I truly do, but my brain just simply will not let me.
Do you find that your thoughts jump from one idea to another when you're alone and quiet, or is it mostly when you're trying to explain these messages to someone else?

Well, Doctor, it’s... it’s mostly when I’m trying to talk to someone else, really. When I’m just sitting alone in the house—maybe in the parlor chair with a cup of tea, or just looking out the window at the frost on the glass—my thoughts feel... well, they feel heavy, and sad, and those warnings are there, but they don't seem to race around quite so much. It's quieter. But the moment I open my mouth to try and share what I'm seeing, that's when the trouble starts. 

I know I’ve said this already, and I really do apologize for going on and on about the same things, but it’s just the perfect example. When I try to explain things, I really do start with just one simple thought, like that piece of mail on the counter or the Sunday church bulletin. I’ll think, 'Just tell Mrs. Gable about the bulletin.' But then, as soon as the words start coming out, it’s like a dam breaks. I end up talking about the quilt patterns I used to make—the Double Wedding Ring pattern, mostly, because of how the circles overlap—and then that makes me think of the birds at the feeder, and the way they screech, and the warnings I feel like they're giving me. 

It all just tumbles out of me, one thing after another, and I can just see it in their faces. I look at them, and their eyes are wide, or they’re looking at their watches, and I know they absolutely don't know what I'm getting at. It’s only when I try to explain it out loud that it all gets so terribly jumbled up like that, and I just end up feeling so foolish and misunderstood.
Do you find your thoughts jumping from one idea to another when you're thinking to yourself, not trying to explain these messages to someone else?

Well, no, Doctor, not really when I am just thinking to myself. Like I was mentioning just a moment ago, when I am all alone, it is quite different. If I am just sitting by myself in the quiet, maybe looking at the mantel clock or just resting my eyes because I feel so terribly drained, my thoughts mostly just... well, they just sit there. They are heavy, and they are sad, but they stay put. 

I know I must sound like I am beating a dead horse here, going over the exact same ground again and again with you, but it really is the honest truth that the jumping only happens when I try to explain things to another living soul. That is the real trigger, you see. In my own head, I have it all lined up perfectly fine. I will think to myself that I am just going to talk about the mail, or maybe that little note in the church bulletin. But the very second I try to put it into words and actually explain things out loud, that is when it all goes sideways. 

I start with that one thought about the mail or the church, and then my tongue just runs completely away from me, and suddenly I end up talking about my old quilt patterns, and the birds outside the window, and those awful warnings I feel. And I can just look right at whoever I am talking to and see it clear as day in their eyes—they absolutely do not know what I am getting at. So no, it is not when I am alone and thinking to myself. It is only the talking out loud that scrambles it all up into such a terrible mess.
Do you find that your thoughts are disorganized or hard to follow when you're not trying to explain these messages to someone else, just thinking to yourself?

Well, Doctor, as I've been trying to say, it really isn't like that when I'm just sitting quietly by myself. I know I'm probably talking your ear off about this, but I just want to make sure I'm explaining it right, because it's so terribly frustrating to me. When it's just me, in my own head, things are mostly just... slow. And sad. Like a dark cloud just sitting there, not moving. 

But you see, it's the talking that does it. It's when I open my mouth. I'll think to myself, 'Alright, Mary, just tell them about the electric bill that came in the mail, or that little announcement they had in the church bulletin on Sunday.' And I really do start out with that one thought. But then, before I can even catch my breath, my mind just takes off running. When I try to explain things, I start with that one thought about the mail or church, and somehow I just completely lose the thread, and I end up talking about those old quilt patterns I used to do—the ones with the little tiny stitches—and then the birds out by the feeder, and the warnings I feel like they're trying to give me. 

And I just keep going, thinking I'm making perfect sense, but then I stop and look at whoever I'm talking to—maybe it's the mailman, or my neighbor—and I can see it. I can just see people don't know what I'm getting at. They look so confused, and then I just feel so foolish and tired. So no, it's not when I'm just thinking to myself. It's only when I try to get the words out to somebody else that it all turns into such a jumbled-up mess.
Do you find your thoughts are disorganized or hard to follow when you're just thinking to yourself, not trying to explain anything to anyone?

Oh, Doctor, I feel like a broken record today, and I really do not mean to be difficult, but it feels like we are just going round and round the mulberry bush on this exact same question. I know I have a habit of talking a bit too much, probably more than I should, but I really thought I had just explained this to you. 

No, my thoughts are not disorganized when I am just sitting by myself in the quiet. When I am alone, my mind is just terribly heavy and still, like a pond that isn't moving. It is the talking that ruins it all. Just like I have been trying to tell you, it is only when I try to explain things to someone else. I will have one perfectly clear thought in my head, like something that came in the morning mail, or a little detail from church. But the moment I try to share it, the words just run completely away from me. I start with that one thought about the mail or the church, and somehow, before I can even stop myself, I end up talking all about my old quilt patterns, and the birds out in the yard, and those awful warnings I keep feeling. 

I just talk and talk, thinking I am making perfect sense, but then I stop and look at their faces. And I can clearly see people don't know what I'm getting at. They look completely lost, and it breaks my heart because I am trying so hard to be understood. So, no, it really is just the speaking out loud to other people that scrambles everything up into such a mess, never when I am just alone with my own thoughts.
Do you experience this disorganized thinking at any other time besides when you're trying to explain these messages to someone?

Doctor, I really don't know how else to say it, and I'm so sorry if I'm testing your patience, but it's just exactly as I've been saying this whole time. It's only when I'm trying to talk to somebody. When I'm alone, sitting in my armchair with my knitting or just looking out the window at the gray sky, my mind is just... well, it's just terribly sad. It doesn't jump around. It just sits there, heavy as lead.

But the minute I open my mouth to try and explain something to someone, that's when it all falls apart. I'll have it all straight in my head, you know? I'll think, 'I just need to tell them about this one thing from the mail, or this one little piece of news from church.' And I start out fine! I really do. But then... it's like a ball of yarn rolling down a hill. I start with that one thought about the mail or church, and before I know it, I'm going on and on about my old quilt patterns—the double wedding ring one, specifically—and then I'm talking about the birds I see outside, and those terrible, heavy warnings I feel like they're bringing. 

And I'll be talking, just pouring it all out, thinking I'm finally making them understand, but then I stop and look at their faces. And it's just awful, Doctor, because I can see people don't know what I'm getting at. They just stare at me, completely lost. So, no, it's never any other time. It's only when I try to explain things to another person that my mind just runs away like that.
Does your thinking ever become disorganized or hard to follow when you're not trying to explain these messages to someone, such as when you're watching TV, reading a book, or doing chores?

Doctor, I really don't mean to be difficult, but I feel like we're just going over the same ground here. I know I talk a lot, probably more than I should, but I really have tried to explain this to you. When I'm watching television—not that there's much good on these days, mostly just those awful news programs that make me so terribly sad—or when I'm folding the laundry, my mind is just... well, it's just heavy. It just sits there, like a stone in my chest. 

It's only when I try to talk to somebody else. That's the only time. Like I was saying before, I'll start out with one simple little thought. Maybe it's about the electric bill that came in the mail, or that little announcement they had in the church bulletin about the bake sale. I start with that one thought, and I try to explain things, but then... well, it just gets completely away from me. I start with the mail or the church, and before I know it, I end up talking about those old quilt patterns I used to make—the ones with the tiny little stitches, you know, the double wedding ring pattern—and then I'm going on about the birds out by the feeder, and the warnings I feel like they're trying to give me. 

And I'll be talking, and I'll think I'm making perfect sense, but then I stop and look at the person I'm talking to. And it's just so embarrassing, Doctor, because I can see people don't know what I'm getting at. They just look at me like I'm speaking a foreign language. So no, it's not when I'm reading a book or doing chores. It's only when I open my mouth to try and explain things to another living soul that it all turns into such a terrible, jumbled-up mess.
Do you find it difficult to follow a plot or storyline when you're reading a book or watching a movie?

Oh, Doctor, I... I really don't mean to sound ungrateful for your help, I truly don't, but I feel like I'm just repeating myself over and over again, like a broken record. We've talked about this so many times now. I know I tend to go on and on, and I'm sorry if I'm taking up too much of your time, but it's exactly like I've been trying to tell you. 

When I'm just sitting quietly, watching a program on the television—though like I said, there's rarely anything good on, mostly just those sad news stories that make my heart feel so heavy—or if I'm trying to read a book, which I don't do as much lately because my mind is just so weighed down with sadness... I can follow the story just fine. The plot makes sense to me. My thoughts don't get all tangled up when I'm just taking things in. 

It's only... it's only when I try to explain things to someone else. That is the only time it happens. I'll have a thought, clear as day, maybe about something I read in a book or saw on one of those programs, or like I keep saying, something from the mail or church. I start out with that one thought, and I try to explain it, but then the words just run away with me. I start with the mail or the church, and then, before I can even catch myself, I end up talking about those quilt patterns again—the double wedding ring one, with the tiny stitches—and the birds out by the feeder, and those awful warnings I feel they're bringing. 

And I'll be talking, and I'll think I'm explaining the plot of the book or the movie perfectly well, but then I stop and look at the person I'm talking to. And I can see it in their eyes, Doctor. I can see people don't know what I'm getting at. They look so confused, and it just breaks my heart. So no, I don't have trouble following a story when I'm just sitting by myself. It's only when I try to talk to someone else that everything turns into such a terrible mess.
Do you have trouble following a conversation or understanding what others are saying to you when you're not trying to explain these messages?

Doctor, I... oh dear, I really don't know how many different ways I can answer this for you. I feel terrible, I truly do, because I know you're just trying to be thorough and ask all your questions, but it's exactly like I've been saying this whole entire time. 

When someone else is talking to me—say, if my neighbor stops by to drop something off, or if I'm listening to the pastor speaking at the front of the sanctuary—I understand them perfectly fine. I hear every word they say. My mind doesn't get confused when I'm just sitting and listening to someone else speak. The sadness is there, of course, always weighing me down like a heavy, wet wool blanket, but I can follow their side of the conversation without any trouble at all. 

It's only... well, it's just like I've said over and over today. It's only when it's my turn to speak. When I try to explain things to them. I'll start out so clearly, with just one simple thought about the mail or the church, and then my mouth just runs away from my brain. Before I can stop myself, I end up talking about those old quilt patterns again, and the birds out the window, and all those heavy warnings I feel like they're bringing. And I can see it right away—I stop and look at their faces, and I can see people don't know what I'm getting at. 

So no, I understand everyone else just fine. It's only my own words that get all tangled up when I try to explain myself.
Do you ever find it difficult to keep your thoughts in order when you're not trying to explain these messages to someone?

Doctor, please... I really, truly don't know what else I can say to make it any clearer. Are you... are you sure you're listening to me? I don't mean to be rude, I was raised better than to snap at a professional, but you keep asking me the exact same question, just using slightly different words every time. It makes a person feel like they aren't being heard at all, and I already feel so invisible and weighed down by this sadness as it is. 

Like I have been telling you, over and over again today... when I am not trying to explain these things to anyone, my thoughts are in perfectly fine order. They don't get jumbled up. It is only—and I really hope you're writing this down in your notes this time—it is only when I try to explain things to people. That's the only time the trouble starts. 

I will start with just one normal little thought, like the mail or the church, and then my tongue just takes over and runs away from me. I end up rambling on about my old quilt patterns, and the birds outside, and those warnings, and then I stop and see the look on people's faces. I can see they don't know what I'm getting at. They look at me like I've lost my senses. So, no, my thoughts are fine when I'm quiet. It's only when I try to explain myself that everything falls apart.
Do you have difficulty organizing your daily tasks or activities when you're not thinking about the messages?

Oh, Doctor... well, that's... that's a different sort of question, isn't it? I suppose... I suppose I haven't really talked about that part of things yet. It's just so hard to get everything out sometimes, with the sadness always there, pulling me down, making everything feel like wading through deep water. 

Organizing my day... well, I try, I really do try to keep things orderly. My mother always taught me that a tidy house makes a tidy mind, and I used to be so good at keeping to a schedule. Breakfast at seven, dishes done by eight, dusting on Tuesdays, baking on Thursdays.
